title: A mixture of sources: praised, dismissed, or merely measured
core: All three describe something made of unlike parts pulled from different origins — no single style, school, or kind runs through it. What separates them is the verdict attached and whether anyone is credited with doing the mixing. One assumes a chooser with taste, one insists no one was choosing at all, and one refuses to say. The mixture is identical; the judgment is the whole difference.

words.nuance: The only one that **compliments**, and it compliments a *person*: **eclectic** implies a selector who ignored genre boundaries and picked each item on its merits. It attaches to taste, collections, and influences — and quietly concedes the person borrowed rather than invented.

The only **noun**, and the only one that says nobody was steering: a **hodgepodge** accumulated by accident. Informal and lightly contemptuous, it calls the result incoherent rather than rich — a policy described this way is being told to start over.

The lab-report word: **heterogeneous** states composition and awards nothing, which is why it often signals trouble — such data won't pool, such a class can't be taught at one level. Note the grammar trap: it describes only the whole, never a single member of it.

exam_note: Context tone decides the answer — approving sentences take *eclectic*, dismissive ones *hodgepodge*, clinical or statistical ones *heterogeneous*; and a blank needing an adjective rules out *hodgepodge* outright.
